Erin, thank you for the time. Let me start with what is not in question: your strength is the customer, and it has never been the problem.
Thank you. I hear a but coming.
There is one. Your region grew eleven percent and your turnover was thirty. Three people left in a year, and two of them told me the same thing on the way out.
Let me guess. That I do everything myself.
That is your blind spot, and you just named it yourself, which is half the work. So here is my opinion: you should delegate the whole reporting, not half of it.
And if the numbers come out wrong, whose name is on them?
Yours. That is exactly why you have to give the authority with the task. And you do not have to do it alone — I will sit in the first two reviews with you.
All right. What I want in return is not a raise. I want the northeast, when it opens.
Then you must step up before it opens, not after. Show me a team that runs without you for one quarter, and that conversation becomes very short.

Three rules for the first two minutes, and then I will stop talking. Rule one. Nothing in a performance review should ever be a surprise. If the person is hearing it for the first time in that room, the manager failed for eleven months, not the employee, and I will say that to any director in this company. Rule two, and this one is about a single word. The word but deletes everything in front of it. If you say your work with the customer is excellent, but your turnover is thirty percent, the person walks out of that room having heard exactly one thing, and it is not the compliment. Say the strength. Stop. Start a new sentence. Rule three, and this is the one people get wrong every single time. Should is your opinion, and it can be discussed. Have to is a rule, and it cannot. If you say should when you actually mean have to, you have just invited a negotiation about something that was never negotiable, and you will lose it.

The best feedback I ever got was one sentence, and I hated it. My director said: your team cannot work without you, and that is not a compliment. That was it. That was the whole thing. I was angry for about a week, because I had spent four years being the person who solves everything, and that was, in my head, the job. What changed my mind was not an argument. It was a holiday. I was away for nine days, and when I came back I counted the decisions that had waited for me. Fourteen. Fourteen decisions, nine days, and not one of them was actually difficult. They waited because everybody knew I would want to look at it. So now I do two things differently. When I give somebody a task, I give the decision away with it, in the same sentence. And I say out loud which things they do not have to bring to me at all, because if I do not say it, they will bring everything, and it will be my fault again.
